title: History 9: Transformers replace U-Nets: DiT and rectified flow

questions.q: You take one Euler step from pure noise on a model trained with rectified flow on random pairs. Where does every sample land?
options: On the mean of the data
questions.answer: On the mean of the data
questions.why: Noise at t = 0 says nothing about which data point it will meet, so the field there is the mean of the data minus x. The lab prints it.

questions.q: Why are the paths of a model trained on random pairs curved, if each training pair is a straight line?
options: Lines cross, and at a crossing least squares learns the average of the right answers
questions.answer: Lines cross, and at a crossing least squares learns the average of the right answers
questions.why: Each point x_t is reached by many pairs, so the model learns E[x1 − x0 | x_t].

questions.q: What does reflow change, and what does it cost?
options: It trains on the pairs the first flow made, so its paths come out straighter. It needs those pairs and a second training run
It uses more Euler steps at no training cost
It swaps the transformer for a U-Net
questions.answer: It trains on the pairs the first flow made, so its paths come out straighter. It needs those pairs and a second training run
questions.why: In the lab straightness falls from 0.7470 to 0.0019 and one-step error falls 13.5 times.

questions.q: HunyuanDiT in ComfyUI is a transformer and predicts v. What does that show?
options: A transformer doesn't have to be a flow model: network and path are separate choices
It is a bug in the model
questions.answer: A transformer doesn't have to be a flow model: network and path are separate choices
questions.why: DiT itself was a diffusion model. SD3 is where the two ideas were put together.

questions.q: You read CONST in ComfyUI. Its sigma 1 is noise, and the model output is what?
options: Noise minus data, the opposite sign to the paper's v
Data minus noise, same as the paper
questions.answer: Noise minus data, the opposite sign to the paper's v
questions.why: calculate_denoised is input − output · sigma. The lab recovers the clean value from it.
